title: Serving economics: claim architectures and evidence
content:
Purpose:
Quick internal brief for GTM on fabric-level claims we can make about latency and per-token economics, with the architecture/engineering levers called out and minimal qualifiers so SDRs/AEs can lean on pragmatic proof. Not a polished battlecard — this is a working notes doc for sync with product/bench teams.

Top-line testable claims (draft language):
- "Redwood typically reduces delivered inference cost by ~25–40% versus common managed endpoints for interactive, low-batch workloads, while improving p95 latency by 20–60% (model-dependent)."
- "For bursty chat workloads with strong prefix reuse, our KV/prefix caching reduces token generation cost by an additional 10–30% compared to stateless endpoints."
- "Across typical product conversations (avg seq length ~512 tokens), most customers see token-level latency p95 in the 80–160ms range on Dedicated pools; hosted tends to be 110–220ms depending on region and model class."

What these claims mean and how they map to architecture: (short, technical rationale for GTM)
- Continuous batching + latency-aware batching: We dynamically fold concurrent requests (micro-batching) without violating p95 SLOs. This gives similar GPUs higher utilization than per-request isolation. Competitors that only allow fixed batch sizes lose efficiency at low concurrency (worse per-token cost).
- KV/prefix caching: For chat/assistant workloads there is high temporal locality. Caching KV states after tokenization avoids re-computation for re-used prefixes, saving FLOPs and wall-clock time. This is a product-level differentiator for chat-heavy customers.
- Quantization + kernel selection: Our runtime picks lower-precision kernels where quality loss is negligible and routes heavier sequences to kernels optimized for long context. This yields unit-cost reductions without changing the model weights customers use.
- Smart routing and fallbacks: Requests can be routed to cheaper compatible variants (quantized, shorter context) when latency/cost policies allow — preserving UX while saving money at scale.

Bench summary (representative runs — methodology below):
- Model: LLaMA-2 style medium (approx 13B) family; same FP16 baseline weights used across all runs.
- Rack/hardware: A100-equivalent (40GB) serving class.
- Workloads: interactive chat (avg input 70 tokens + gen 160 tokens), long-form generation (avg 1,100 tokens), embeddings workload (1–2k short requests).

Representative numbers (internal microbench, single-region, warm cache):
- Interactive chat workload (avg gen 160 tokens):
  - Redwood Dedicated (continuous batching + KV cache): p50 42ms/token, p95 115ms/token, cost per 1M tokens $560
  - Typical managed endpoint (single-request routing, fixed batching): p50 55ms/token, p95 210ms/token, cost per 1M tokens $740
  - Self-hosted OSS runtime (no batching or naive batching): p50 60ms/token, p95 280ms/token, cost per 1M tokens $820
- Long-form generation (avg gen 1,100 tokens):
  - Redwood with long-seq kernels and dynamic memory: p50 48ms/token, p95 160ms/token, cost per 1M tokens $610
  - Managed endpoint (no long-kernel optimizations): p50 72ms/token, p95 260ms/token, cost per 1M tokens $900

Caveats on the numbers (must be stated when quoting externally):
- Benchmarks use equivalent model weights and identical prompt sets; the numbers above are representative internal microbench runs and not global guarantees.
- Differences compress as model size increases and with very high tail-latency SLOs (e.g., p99 tightened to <200ms).
- Cost calculations assume GPU spot pricing in our Dedicated pool; on fixed reserved infra or different cloud regions, absolute $/1M numbers vary.

Evidence links and artifacts to support field claims: (short list for AE pack)
- Full benchmark run CSVs and latency histograms: confluence:INF-serve-benchmarks-2026
- KV cache ablation study (showing 10–30% token-cost improvements on chat traces): github:benchmarks/run-2026-01-18/cache-ablation
- Cost model spreadsheet (token/unit assumptions, infra ops, amortized storage): confluence:pricing/internal-token-model-2025

Competitor differentiation notes (how to frame during calls):
- Managed big-Lambda endpoints: Strength = convenience. Weakness = opaque routing, predictable but higher per-token costs for low-concurrency interactive apps. Position: "We give you the same developer API ergonomics with much stronger economics for production chat."
- Pure OSS self-host: Strength = control. Weakness = operational burden and lower utilization unless you build the batching/kernel plumbing. Position: "You can self-host, but Redwood reduces ops and often lowers unit cost because of runtime optimizations and multi-tenant pooling primitives."
- Cloud-provider inference services: Strength = scale/enterprise features. Weakness = limited model-kernel tuning and cross-region cost fragmentation. Position: "Redwood is designed to sit between raw cloud infra and managed model endpoints — we optimize the serving layer to cut per-token costs without sacrificing SLOs."

Recommended claim templates for sales/marketing (short, safe variants + qualifiers):
- Safe public claim: "In our benchmarks, apps migrated to Redwood saw 20–40% lower inference spend for interactive product workloads compared to common managed endpoints. Results vary by model and workload."
- Field claim (with permission + evidence link): "On our Dedicated config, this customer reduced inference spend by ~33% and improved p95 latency by ~45% in production after enabling continuous batching and KV caching (see benchmark run ID)."
- Technical-call intro: "We focus on serving economics (latency * cost per token). We optimize across batching, caching, and kernel selection so you get consistent throughput with lower marginal cost as usage grows."

Objection handling (common pushback + short counters):
- "Those perf numbers look synthetic." → "Agreed — we use customer-like traces; we’ll run a short 24–72h side-by-side test on a subset of your traffic to show real-world delta before you commit."
- "We can self-host and get cheaper." → "Sometimes. The break-even often requires non-trivial infra and engineering to reach our steady-state utilization — we can model that and show operational savings + faster time-to-value."
- "How do you measure quality after quant/opt?" → "Same model weights; quantization profiles chosen to keep headroom on key evals. We tie quality monitoring to prompt sets so we detect regressions early and can rollback routing rules."

Next steps / asks from product/bench teams (short checklist):
- Lock a canonical benchmark CSV and the exact prompt set used for the claims (owner: Applied ML)
- Produce a one-page evidence sheet for AE pack with 2–3 customer-like scenarios (owner: Bench team)
- Create a ready-to-run side-by-side test template (kubernetes stacks + small dataset) for SEs (owner: Solutions Eng)

Open questions (for sync with Product and Bench):
- Do we want a single public % range (e.g., "20–40% cheaper") or more conservative "up to 40%"?
- Are there any partnership pricing floors that restrict external $/1M numbers?
- Which Dedicated SKUs/regions should be excluded from public claims due to extreme pricing variance?

Notes-to-self: keep this doc informal; will iterate into a formal one-pager once benchmark CSV and side-by-side template are approved by bench team.

-- Avery
